sentences.text: Tiktaalik roseae is the sole species of an extinct genus of lobe-finned fish that lived roughly 375 million years ago.
Individuals ranged in total length from 1.25 to 2.75 meters, with the largest known specimens having lower jaws measuring 31 centimeters.
Its head featured a low, flat shape resembling a salamander rather than typical fish.
The specific name roseae was chosen to honor an anonymous donor.
Fossils were first uncovered in 2004 on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut, Canada.
Edward B. Daeschler, Neil H. Shubin, and Farish A. Jenkins Jr. described the find in the April 6, 2006 issue of Nature, where it was quickly hailed as a classic transitional form.
Indentations on the skull suggest the animal may have possessed primitive lungs alongside gills.
Researchers propose that Tiktaalik flexed its proto-limbs on stream beds and pulled itself onto shores, aided by a robust pelvic girdle found in 2014.
A 2008 study revealed it was building structures to hold its weight on land and inhale air, marking a vital step toward terrestrial existence.
Originally placed in the group Elpistostegalia, Tiktaalik was formally described by Daeschler, Shubin, and Jenkins in 2006.
It is viewed as a transitional fossil bridging fish and tetrapods, much like Archaeopteryx connects reptiles and birds.
Living during the Frasnian stage of the Late Devonian, it inhabited Ellesmere Island when it was part of the equatorial continent Laurentia.
The environment featured warm shallows where deciduous plants shed leaves, attracting small prey that larger fish struggled to catch.
Three main theories exist regarding digit evolution: symmetric development from radials, a neomorphic origin as a new structure, or homology to postaxial radials.
Scientists debate whether Panderichthys is closer to tetrapods than Tiktaalik or if their similarities stem from convergent evolution, as argued in a 2008 paper by Boisvert et al.
